## Seas, interception and outlaws

**Seas, interception and outlaws (interception on the road, pirates and bandits decided, build order items 7 and 11; deniable attacks decided, needing no rule; finer seas decided, build order item 7).**

- **Finer seas (decided 21 October 2026, built with the blockade in build order item 7).** Five sea zones against 41 land provinces is too coarse: Cyprus's two provinces alone touch four of the five, so under the blockade rule Alashiya, starting with one fleet, could never guard its own coast. The seas are redrawn after how Late Bronze Age seafaring worked.

  How it worked:
  - **Ships kept to the coasts.** Hulls were light, with one square sail, and sailed well only with the wind behind or abeam, so voyages went coast to coast in daytime stages with island stops, and long open crossings were the hard legs, taking days.
  - **The sea had a season.** Sailing ran roughly April to October in the eastern Mediterranean; winter was unsuited to it.
  - **Currents ran counterclockwise:** north along the Levant, west along southern Anatolia. A voyage from Cyprus home to the Aegean went by the Anatolian coast rather than straight back, so routes were easier one way than the other.
  - **Naval power was raiding, blockading harbours and seizing ships.** In the Amarna letters Arwad's ships lay off the coast to stop grain reaching Ṣumur (EA 98), blockaded its shore with the sons of ʿAbdi-Aširta so Rib-Hadda could not relieve it (EA 104–105), and threatened his own ships at sea. Blockades were of particular harbours and coasts, not of whole seas, and ships served mostly as transports and raiders, joining sieges from the sea.
  - **No island could guard every shore.** The king of Alashiya complained that "men of Lukki, year by year, seize villages in my own country" (EA 38): raiders landed where no ships stood.

  What the game does:
  - **Coastal waters per coastal province.** Each coastal province gets waters of its own, its harbour and shore; two neighbouring provinces with a short shared coast may share them. Both Cypriot provinces, Enkomi and the western one ("Map review"), have their own.
  - **Landing and supply need the coastal waters there.** Troops land, and a besieged coastal city or island is supplied, only where the enemy's fleets do not hold that province's waters. A fleet holding a harbour's waters blockades it, as Arwad did Ṣumur.
  - **A few open-sea crossings** link coastal waters, such as Cyprus to Anatolia or to the Levant, and Crete to the Aegean coasts. They are hard to stop anyone in and slow to cross, and the fight happens where one comes ashore.
  - **The sailing season.** In the winter season open crossings are closed or much riskier, and coastal hops riskier; first guesses, tuned in item 18.
  - **Currents as data.** A crossing can take longer one way than the other, so the counterclockwise circuit shapes trade and war without a rule of its own.

  The exact division is a first guess, likely 15 to 25 sea zones in all, tested in the script games and reported. Pirates, patrols and interception at sea ("Pirates are bands at sea", item 7's interception) then happen in particular waters rather than across half the sea. Sources: [EA 38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amarna_letter_EA_38); Emanuel, ["Arwad and the miši ships"](https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/AUTHORS/SeaPeoples/Emanuel2020-Arwad&Misi.pdf) (2020), on EA 98, 101, 104–105 and 149; Querci, [appendix on Late Bronze Age sailing routes](https://edizionicafoscari.it/media/pdf/books/978-88-6969-858-3/978-88-6969-858-3-ch-09_T7x4gH3.pdf), on ships, seasons, currents and routes.
- **Interception on the road. (Decided 19 October 2026 in a simple form, build order item 7: a route is a chain of provinces, and a hostile army, an outlaw band or the lawlessness of a place on it may stop a traveller, with the odds shaped by his skill, his escort, policing and roads. The segment scheme below is not needed.)** If travel becomes distance-based and takes several seasons, two movements crossing on the same route must meet, decided deterministically (for example by dividing each route into segments per season). Two armies fight; an army may capture a hostile envoy or shipment; two envoys pass unless one reports what it saw. Nature can stop a traveller too (decided 21 October 2026), in the same check and from the land and climate profile and the season: storms at sea, worst in winter and on long crossings; passes closed by snow; floods on river routes; supplies running out in the desert. Revised 21 October 2026, now that pace varies ("What sets a company's pace"): a traveller may cross several provinces in a season, so the check falls on one province of the stretch he crossed, picked by the share of the season he spent in each. A fast company cannot slip through a bandit province untouched, and a slow one is not singled out by where it happens to stop.
- **A road belongs to the land it crosses (decided 21 October 2026).** Nobody owns a road: every stretch of it lies in some province, and that province's holder rules it, with its policing, its tolls and its road check. A connection between two provinces is two halves, with the border halfway by default, and map data moves it where the terrain says otherwise: a pass or a stretch of desert belongs to the side it lies on. So the time a traveller spends on a connection counts in the province whose half he is on, which is the share of the season the road check weighs (above); goods pay a toll on crossing into another holder's half ("Tolls and smuggling"); and a road built jointly with a neighbour is each side's own half ("Anyone can fund a project"). A door is a province, not a road, so every door has a holder ("Arrivals come through doors"). Built with the routes in item 7.
- **Choosing a route (decided 21 October 2026).** The traveller chooses his route from what he knows, and the sender may lay it down in the errand's mandate. He knows threats only from news that has reached him, so old news makes bad routes. A bold traveller takes the short, dangerous road and a careful one the long, safe one ("Bold or careful, one goal"): script travellers weigh time against risk by formula, and model travellers choose for themselves. Built with travel in item 7.
- **Pirates and bandits. (Decided 19 October 2026, build order item 11.)** The Lukka raided Alashiya, and the vassal letters are full of the Habiru, outlaws and mercenaries the vassals accused each other of using. Banditry and piracy rise where an owner spends little on patrols and garrisons, and with poverty, war and disaster. They intercept envoys, gold shipments and caravans, giving policing a real price.
- **Deniable attacks. (Decided 19 October 2026: possible, and needing no rule of its own. With outlaws on the roads, gold that can be handed over and characters dealing with each other, a king can pay a band and deny it; a captured outlaw may confess who paid him, as caught spies confess their master.)** A king may quietly sponsor bandits or pirates against a rival's envoys and then blame the Habiru; the victim cannot prove who did it. This fits the core of the game: an attack whose author cannot be proven.
- Outlaws are a world force run by scripts, so they cost no model calls. They belong after sieges and distance-based travel, since they only matter once routes take time.

**What sets a company's pace (decided 21 October 2026).** One rule for everything that moves, armies, caravans, couriers and envoys alike, so a big army is slow for the same reasons as a big caravan. A company moves at the pace of its slowest part, so a king chooses between one large, safe convoy and several small, quick ones. Its pace comes from:

- **The land it crosses:** terrain, roads and the season, as decided.
- **Its size:** a long column is slow to move and to water, and draws attention.
- **Its load against what it can carry:** a company carrying less than it could moves faster.
- **Its animals:** donkeys are the pack animals of the age (an Old Assyrian donkey carried some 65 kg of tin and cloth), and oxcarts carry heavy loads slowly. Horses are rare and go into chariots, which speed messengers and envoys on good roads rather than caravans. There are no camels, which were not yet in use in the region.
- **Water:** in arid land a company can be only as large as the wells allow, which is why the Ways of Horus across Sinai were a chain of forts with wells.
- **River crossings:** fords close in the flood season and ferries hold a column up; the map data already holds the crossings.
- **Fodder:** in winter or desert the animals' fodder is carried, which eats into the load.
- **Pace as a choice:** a forced march is faster, and men and animals drop along the way, a real decision for an army racing to relieve a siege.
- **The leader:** a character who knows the road leads faster; men alone keep the average pace.
- **Sneaking:** travel off the road, to avoid tolls or policing, is slower, so smuggling buys secrecy with time.
- **On water:** current, wind and the sailing season ("Finer seas", "Rivers").

**Built once, switched on as the game grows.** Item 7b builds the rule as one function with every factor as a term that reads data; a term whose system does not exist yet stays neutral, neither speeding nor slowing, until the item that brings that system turns it on, with the benchmarks recorded before and after and the item's usual test of scripts that use the feature against scripts that ignore it. So travel is written once and never rewritten, and no system is built before its time. Progress accumulates: a company advances a number of whole points along its route each season, and what it does not use carries over, so a factor worth days or weeks shifts an arrival by days or weeks over a long road, not only when it happens to push it into the next season. All terms are integer data with first guesses, tuned in item 18.

**Map review (decided 21 October 2026, built with the redrawn seas in build order item 7).** The map's density follows the politics: the Levant, where most of the Amarna letters were written, is finely divided, and Anatolia and Mesopotamia coarsely. That is right for the game, with these corrections:

- **Distance, not steps.** Each connection gets a length, weighted by its terrain, so travel time follows the ground rather than the number of provinces between. Two steps on the Anatolian plateau cover far more ground than two along the Levantine coast.
- **The northern Syrian theatre.** Northern Syria was the battleground of Hatti, Mitanni and Egypt in exactly this period. Add Aleppo (Halab), the great city of the north, in Mitanni's sphere until the Hittites took it, and Qatna, whose king Akizzi wrote several of the letters; and, since the redrawn seas need them, Sidon and the island of Arwad. Ṣumur, Egypt's base on Amurru's coast and the city of the Arwad blockade, is built both ways and the better one kept: as Amurru's harbour, or as a province of its own. The only argument against its own province is how crowded the coast becomes on a phone, so the choice follows the map's readability and the script games, and the report says which was kept and why. The long Carchemish–Qadesh link then gives way to links through them.
- **Places in their own time.** Mari was destroyed by Hammurabi around 1760 BCE and by 1346 was a small place in the land of Hana, so the middle Euphrates province takes a name of its period and loses Mari's fortress walls. Kanesh mattered mostly in the earlier Old Assyrian age, so its province takes a name of the Hittite period. Ekallatum is likewise best known from the Old Assyrian age, and Tamassos from the Iron Age: Cyprus keeps two provinces, each named for a town of the period like every other province. The east keeps Enkomi, the great harbour town and probably the seat of the king of Alashiya. The west, with Morphou Bay, where ships from Anatolia and Crete came ashore, and the copper hills, takes the name of a Late Bronze Age town inside the area it covers: Toumba tou Skourou if it centres on Morphou Bay and the copper hills, Palaepaphos (Kouklia) if it reaches the southwest coast, Kalavasos if it takes in the south; the builder draws the province first and chooses its name from the sources. No region is removed; only names out of their time change. The builder chooses the names from the sources and records the basis.
- **Connections of the right kind.** The routes from the middle Euphrates to Damascus and Qadesh cross the Syrian desert and become desert connections. Kanesh–Carchemish crosses mountains and gets a pass, as Kanesh–Kizzuwatna has.
- **Nubia.** Kush, south of Thebes, was the source of Egypt's gold, the gold every other Great King asked for ("gold is as plentiful as dust in your land", Tushratta wrote), and was governed directly by Egypt's viceroy, the King's Son of Kush. It joins the map as Egyptian land: the Nile runs through it, its land is arid and carries few people, and its yield is mostly gold. Scoring measures each power against its own start, so a richer Egypt also faces a higher bar; the balance pass watches Egypt's start, as "Opening relations as they were" already asks.

Also:

- **What earns a place.** A province is a polity or administrative centre that acts in the period's diplomacy or war, not a town above some size. By that bar add Alalakh (Mukish), a Mitanni vassal and Idrimi's city; Nuhashshe, fought over in Suppiluliuma's Syrian wars; two provinces for southern Canaan's highlands, Jerusalem under Abdi-Heba and Shechem under Labaya, rival vassals of Egypt who accused each other before Pharaoh of joining the Habiru, which is the kind of story the game is built to produce (if the coast and highlands grow too crowded on a phone, the same test as for Ṣumur decides); and Arrapha, Mitanni's eastern vassal, whose town of Nuzi left the adoption tablets. The map then has about 50 to 52 land provinces, most of the new ones in Syria and Canaan, so the visual overhaul must make the Levant easy to zoom on a phone. Kumidi in the Beqaa, the third of Egypt's administrative centres in Canaan beside Gaza and Ṣumur, is judged by the same bar.
- **Historical routes and times.** Connections follow known routes: the coast road to Egypt, the King's Highway east of the Jordan, the Euphrates route and the Taurus passes. Travel times are calibrated against journeys the sources attest where they give them, and the builder records what each time is based on.
- **The edges of the map.** Places that acted on the Great Kings belong on the map even at its edge, or a power loses part of who it was:
  - **Dilmun and the Gulf.** Dilmun (Bahrain) was Babylonia's in this period, under a Kassite governor, so it starts as Babylonia's land, with a Gulf sea zone from Ur that Elam's coast also touches. It gives Babylonia its sea and its route towards Magan's copper; trade (decided 21 October 2026) gives that route its full meaning ("A trade system").
  - **The Kaska lands.** North of Hattusa lived the Kaska, raiders without a king who burned Hattusa itself in the generation before 1346. They start as a lawless land of loose men, like Lukka, and are Hatti's standing threat from the north ("People of the land", "Bands are a character's soldiers").
  - **The Sutean steppe.** The nomads of the Syrian steppe raided travellers and served as hired fighters. The desert routes from the middle Euphrates cross their land, which starts as desert with loose men and no ruler.
  - **Off the map, as the far ends of routes:** Magan, Punt and Elam's eastern lands beyond Susa; with the economy, these are edge markets ("Edge markets").
  - **The western edge:** Ahhiyawa and Millawanda (Miletus) mattered more in the following century; they stay an edge to watch ("A trade system").
- **Roads are paid for by those who build them.** A road (build order item 15) is built by the gold and labour put into it. When neighbours build one together, the split is agreed on a sealed tablet and, like every term, is only words. Who owns it is set by "A road belongs to the land it crosses", so building through another's land is an investment he can take, which is why it needs passage rights (item 9) and trust.

Places and dates here are from memory where no source is linked; the builder checks them against the sources and records any doubt.

**Grounded in the sources (decided 21 October 2026, build order item 6+).** Before the map, the people of the land and the opening relations are built, a research pass gathers what the sources say about the world in 1346 BCE, so the start is as historically accurate as the evidence allows. It writes dossiers in the repository (`docs/history/`), every claim with its source and how sure it is:

- **Politics:** who ruled where in 1346, who was whose vassal, and what the letters show of each relation ("Opening relations as they were"). One chronology for everything, the one the game's dates already use, with the doubts recorded, such as which kings reigned in Hatti and Arzawa that year.
- **Geography:** routes, distances and journey times the sources attest, terrain, passes, rivers, coasts and harbours ("Map review", "Finer seas").
- **Environment and seasons:** each region's climate, its rivers' floods, its sowing and harvest, droughts and plagues on record ("Land and climate", "Rivers", "Seasons").
- **People and settlement:** population estimates by region, the sizes of towns and the shares of farmers, soldiers and townspeople ("People of the land"). Ancient numbers are uncertain, so the dossiers give ranges, and the game is calibrated within them and against today's yields.
- **Economy:** what each land produced and traded: Nubia's gold, Cyprus's copper, the tin and textile routes.
- **People:** every attested person of the period who could appear in the game: kings, vassal rulers, envoys, officials, scribes and merchants, with what is known of each ("Attested characters").

**The letters come first.** The Amarna letters themselves, in scholarly translation, are the primary source for everything above, and for three things only they can give:

- **Relationships:** who calls whom brother, who complains of whom, the grievances over gold, brides and detained envoys. They seed the starting sympathies, grievances and facts of rulers and characters ("A past before the game, then a past made in play").
- **The voice of the age:** how a request is phrased, how a grievance is made, the greetings, prostrations and gift lists ("Voice of the age" in the main tab).
- **The norms of the time:** brotherhood among the Great Kings, gifts answered with gifts, envoys held as leverage, a vassal's duty to report.

Treaties, the Hittite archives, the tablets of Ugarit and archaeology fill in where the letters are silent.

**Style, not strategy.** The letters set how people speak and what is normal, never what they want. Every king and character still plays to win ("Stakes, not dispositions"): a vassal can fall at the king's feet seven times and seven times and betray him in the same season, and a Great King can call another brother while working for his ruin, as the letters themselves show. The period's deference is a form, not a surrender. The second agent simulation showed how easily models slide into accommodation, so the norms are taught as tools of play, never as limits on it.

**A reference to use creatively, not a script.** The letters may be quoted in full where that fits: in the dossiers, the primer and the requests, within each request's size budget. Where a verbatim line does not fit the moment, it is reshaped to fit, or the letters' general style is matched instead, whichever serves the context better. A quotation shows how things were said and what was normal; it never decides what anyone does. That is decided by the goal and by each character's own road to it: the strategy the engine chooses from his traits and gives him in his starting prompt ("How the strategy is made", "Bold or careful, one goal"). The primer and the quotations only shape how he speaks on that road.

The dossiers feed build order items 7, 10, 10+, 11, 11+ and 17, which cite them. Where the sources are silent, the builder says so and takes a reasonable first guess, marked as such.
